item.title: Is Saudi Arabia expanding its ballistic missile programme?
item.description:
Is Saudi Arabia expanding its ballistic missile programme?

Saudi Arabia is believed to be expanding its Chinese-designed ballistic missile arsenal as it faces an unprecedented barrage of missile and drone attacks from Yemen's Houthi forces.

Satellite imagery analysed by American researchers suggests the kingdom is expanding its ballistic missile plant at al-Duwadimi in Riyadh Province to build larger solid-fuel missiles capable of carrying heavier payloads across greater distances.

Fighting between the kingdom and the Iran-aligned Yemeni group has intensified since July, shattering a UN-brokered truce that had largely held since 2022. 

The Houthis have stepped up missile and drone attacks on Saudi cities, airports and energy infrastructure, retaliating for what they call a Saudi "blockade" of ports and airports in Houthi-controlled areas of Yemen.

Analysts have told Middle East Eye that the renewed confrontation with the Houthis has given the kingdom's arsenal added significance.

Read more: Is Saudi Arabia expanding its ballistic missile programme?

item.title: Trump says Iran would be hit with 'no hesitation' if it threatens allies, US ships
item.description:
Trump says Iran would be hit with 'no hesitation' if it threatens allies, US ships

US President Donald Trump said he could use military force against Iran with "no hesitation" if Washington's ships and allies are threatened.  

During an interview with the Salem News Channel, the US president was asked whether he would hesitate to use force to stop Iran from "terrorising our allies and our ships,".

"No hesitation. We’re doing very well with it right now," Trump answered. "But the answer is, if I saw things going the other way, I would do that, and it’s possible I would do it right now."

Trump claimed the US has suffered no losses in recent months, despite reports and official figures indicating that over a dozen soldiers have died as  a result of the war on Iran.

"We haven’t lost a soldier in five months, and we control the Gulf... Totally control it," he said.

item.title: Ghalibaf says 'ball is in America's court' for US-Iran peace talks
item.description:
Ghalibaf says 'ball is in America's court' for US-Iran peace talks

Iran's parliament speaker, Mohammad Bagher Ghalibaf, said in an interview with Al Jazeera that Tehran has no desire to continue the war with the US, but that the ball is in Washington’s court for peace talks.

Ghalibaf said that Iran provided the US with a clear and transparent response outlining its demands, but the Trump administration has not yet responded.

An agreement with Washington is possible, he added, provided it adheres to what was previously agreed upon and refrains from actions that undermine trust and excessive demands.

He said that Iran is determined to move beyond the state of “no war, no peace” through negotiations or sustainable deterrence, and accused Washington of imposing a siege on the country by blocking access to food and hindering trade and healthcare services.

“As the saying goes, the ball is in America’s court.” Iran's parliament speaker, Mohammad Bagher Ghalibaf, said in an interview with Al Jazeera that Tehran has no desire to continue the war with the US, but that the ball is in Washington’s court for peace talks. https://t.co/phdAbTbmQ8

item.title: Iran’s IRGC says it targeted US radar in Bahrain

Iran’s IRGC says it targeted US radar in Bahrain

Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) announced that its forces targeted a US early-warning radar in Bahrain in retaliation to an attack on a telecommunications tower in Iran’s Sirik.

"This serves as a serious warning to the aggressor enemy to cease its aerial provocations and oil smuggling in the Strait of Hormuz. Should these violations and acts of aggression recur, the IRGC Aerospace Force stands in full readiness to engage without limits," the IRGC was quoted as saying by local media.

item.title: Oil slicks seen from space: the devastating impact of boat strikes on fragile Gulf ecosystems
item.description:
Since the US war on Iran began in February, there have been hundreds of oil spills, posing a ‘generational’ threat to wildlife

The vast, dark slicks in the strait of Hormuz are visible from space. Throughout October, oil tankers were struck by missiles or sea mines in the waterway and spilled crude into the sea. The pollution has spread across the Gulf, contaminating coastlines and threatening to cause lasting damage to marine ecosystems that are home to dolphins, sea turtles and countless species of fish.

Eight months into the war between the US and Iran, one of the world’s busiest oil shipping routes has become a battlefield and the centre of a growing environmental disaster.
